name: Habitat for Humanity International: international programme (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: Habitat's work in more than 60 countries, by region at the shares of the result at the defaults (Africa 52%, Asia and the Pacific 26%, Europe and the Middle East 12%, Latin America and the Caribbean 10%), each region's share spread equally over the stand-in countries whose survey consumption the build reads (a judgment).
summary: Habitat for Humanity International (HFHI) spent $75.5 million in the year to June 2025 ($74 million without the Home Equals advocacy booked in the same line, counted in the awareness model) helping families outside the US build, extend and repair homes with Habitat national organisations in more than 60 countries (mostly incremental building and repairs, about 470,000 people across the network), and working with lenders and building-material firms so that low-income households can buy housing loans and products (2.4 million people in Habitat's count). Valued as the net housing subsidy families receive on the site's log-income scale, at the household-survey consumption of Habitat's families in each region, plus a small surplus for borrowers and buyers of products, it does about 0.07 years of healthy life per $1,000. It is well below cash transfers because only about 17 cents of each dollar reaches families as housing (HFHI's transfers to partners are 31% of the programme's cost with overhead, and the national organisations it funds spend part on their own staff), close to 60% of the families are in middle-income Latin America, Europe and the Middle East, housing is an in-kind transfer, and both branches (direct housing and market development) are discounted for missing data: HFHI publishes no count of the families its own money reached, no subsidy per family and no split of its spending by type of work. Those are the biggest uncertainties, with the families' consumption.

rows.explainer: Habitat for Humanity International's (HFHI) programme spending outside the US and Canada in the year to 30 June 2025: grants and house-building transfers to Habitat national organisations and partners ($31.4 million), its area and country offices' staff ($28.1 million), professional services ($5.9 million) and the rest. It pays for homes, incremental improvements, repairs and disaster shelter that families build with Habitat (the direct branch), and for the Terwilliger Center's and national offices' work with banks, microfinance institutions and building-material firms (the market branch). Public awareness and education, with HFHI's housing advocacy, is modelled separately (habitat-for-humanity-charityevals-awareness).

Share of HFHI's international transfers that fund direct housing (not market work)
rows.explainer: HFHI's transfers to national organisations and partners pay mostly for homes, incremental building, repairs and disaster shelter; some fund national offices' market and housing-finance work. HFHI publishes no split. 0.8, range 0.6 to 0.95. The market branch is paid for mostly by HFHI's own staff (the Terwilliger Center), so it isn't tied to this row.

rows.label: Share of an independent national organisation's housing spending that reaches families as materials, skilled labour and subsidy
rows.explainer: One question, for the national organisations HFHI funds but doesn't consolidate: the share of a national organisation's spending of HFHI money that goes to materials, skilled labour and families' subsidy rather than its own staff and offices (families' repayments are netted only in the subsidy per family). Habitat for Humanity Poland's audited 2024 accounts are the one national organisation's we could read: of PLN 31.3 million of costs, PLN 24.7 million (79%) were its statutory programme work, the rest administration (PLN 3.4 million), its trading arm (PLN 1.8 million), financing (PLN 0.8 million) and other operating costs (PLN 0.6 million); the programme figure still includes its own programme staff (70 employees) and, in 2024, refugee shelter and a social rental agency more than construction. So 79% is the ceiling of what can reach families; with programme staff and supervision taken out, 0.6, range 0.4 to 0.8. Cross-checks: HFHI's own US programme passes 65% of its spending to affiliates as cash and products (audited statement p. 7); a single-purpose cash charity reaches 84% (GiveDirectly).

rows.label: Share of HFHI's international transfers spent by the national organisations consolidated in its accounts
rows.explainer: HFHI's audited statements consolidate eleven national organisations registered as part of HFHI (note 2), with Habitat for Humanity-Middle East and MicroBuild India. For them, the transfers line is their own direct spending on vendors, materials and families (transfers between them and HFHI are eliminated), and their staff are already in the $28.1 million salaries line. Eleven of Habitat's 60-plus countries, among them some of the larger programmes: 0.3, range 0.1 to 0.5. No split of the transfers by recipient is published (the Form 990's foreign grants schedule could anchor it in a later build); the range carries the doubt, worth about ±9% of the result.

rows.label: Share of a consolidated national organisation's transfers that reach families as materials, labour and subsidy
rows.explainer: Their staff are outside this line, so nearly all of it is materials, contractors and families' subsidy; some is rent, vehicles and other costs booked as payments to vendors. 0.9, range 0.8 to 1.

rows.label: Housing value reaching families as a share of the programme's total cost
rows.formula: intl_transfers / cost_total * dir_transfers_share * (consolidated_transfer_share * consolidated_delivery_share + (1 - consolidated_transfer_share) * nso_delivery_share)
rows.explainer: HFHI's transfers to partners over the programme's cost with overhead, times the share of them for direct housing and the share reaching families: nearly all of what the consolidated national organisations spend (their staff are in HFHI's salaries line), the delivery share of what the independent ones spend. About 17 cents per dollar.

rows.label: Net housing subsidy per family in the direct branch (US$)
rows.explainer: No average is published. The direct branch is mostly incremental building (265,445 people) and repairs (177,520), with few new or rehabilitated homes (29,935): Habitat's FY2025 individuals-served table. A floor, a latrine, a roof or a room typically costs a few hundred to $2,000 in materials and skilled labour (cement floors and improved stoves in Habitat's Global Village work; a $1,000 to $2,000 incremental loan), a new core house $5,000 to $15,000, disaster shelter kits much less. Weighted by people: 0.06 × $10,000 + 0.56 × $1,500 + 0.38 × $1,000 = about $1,800 at full cost; families contribute labour and repay some loans, so $1,500 net, range $700 to $3,500.

rows.label: Families HFHI's direct-housing spending reached
rows.explainer: HFHI's own dollars only: national organisations and other donors fund the rest of the network's international work, so this is far fewer families than Habitat's own count for the network: 472,900 people (about 130,000 households) in new and rehab construction, incremental construction and repairs across Latin America and the Caribbean, Europe and the Middle East, Africa and Asia-Pacific (FY2025 annual report, individuals served).

source.quote: Market development 304,150 (Latin America and the Caribbean); 485,515 (Europe and Middle East); 508,100 (Africa); 1,146,465 (Asia and the Pacific)

rows.explainer: Market development across the four regions (2,444,230): people in households that bought housing loans, building materials or services from lenders and firms Habitat works with, Habitat's own count from partners' reports with no stated method. The low end is the Form 990's 'nearly 300,000 households' for the Terwilliger Center's partners alone (× 3.5 people), in case the regional count includes others' customers or double counts; MicroBuild Fund 1 was winding down (one open investment by year end) and adds little in FY2025. Professional services (49,985: land, titling and construction advice) buy nothing, so they are left out here and counted with tenure security in unmodelled_benefits_adj; civil-society facilitation (12,990) is the local organising behind Home Equals, valued in the awareness model.

rows.explainer: For reading; each branch uses its own.

rows.label: Years a direct-housing improvement keeps its value
rows.explainer: A cement floor, roof or latrine lasts about 10 to 15 years, a core house longer, a shelter kit a year or two. The result barely moves with it: the yearly value is spread over the same years it is discounted over.

rows.label: Value of the direct subsidy per person per year (US$)
rows.explainer: The subsidy as an even yearly flow of better housing over the years it lasts (its present value equals the subsidy at the shared rate), per person.

rows.label: ln(consumption) gain per person, direct branch, discounted
rows.formula: lac_share * dir_ln_gain_lac + eme_share * dir_ln_gain_eme + afr_share * dir_ln_gain_afr + (1 - lac_share - eme_share - afr_share) * dir_ln_gain_ap
rows.explainer: The regions' gains weighted by where the direct-housing families are, so the log curve is applied at each region's own consumption.

rows.label: Market-branch households' consumption relative to direct-housing families'
rows.explainer: Households that take housing loans from microfinance institutions and buy building materials from firms are better off than direct-housing families: borrowers need steady incomes. 1.7 times, range 1.2 to 2.5.

rows.label: Market-branch households' consumption per person (US$)
rows.formula: mkt_vs_dir_consumption * (mkt_lac * cons_fam_lac + mkt_eme * cons_fam_eme + mkt_afr * cons_fam_afr + mkt_ap * cons_fam_ap) / (mkt_lac + mkt_eme + mkt_afr + mkt_ap)
rows.explainer: For reading: the regional consumption of Habitat's families weighted by where the market branch's people are, times the market households' higher consumption; the gain itself is taken region by region.

rows.label: Share of the market branch's households that took a housing loan (the rest bought products or services)
rows.explainer: Habitat's market count mixes housing-microfinance borrowers (MicroBuild's investees and the national offices' partner lenders: $230 million lent to 236,000 households over MicroBuild Fund 1's life, FY2025 annual report) with buyers of building materials, construction services and technical advice from the Terwilliger Center's firms ('nearly 300,000 households' received 'products or services' from its partners, Form 990). No split is published; borrowers are the smaller part of the yearly count: 0.4, range 0.2 to 0.7.

rows.label: Value to a household of a housing loan through Habitat's partner lenders (US$, present value)
rows.explainer: Borrowers pay for their loans, so the benefit is their surplus over the next-best option. A typical housing microloan is about $1,000 (MicroBuild: $230 million over 236,000 households) over one to three years; 10 to 15 points less interest than informal lenders for two years is $200 to $300, but most borrowers' alternative is a general microloan or slower self-financing. The trials of new microcredit access find modest gains: borrowing rises, much of it replacing other credit, and consumption barely moves (Banerjee, Karlan and Zinman 2015, six randomized evaluations; Meager 2019, a Bayesian meta-analysis of seven, AEJ: Applied Economics, effects on consumption near zero and uncertain). Best $150, range $30 to $400.

rows.label: Value to a household of a building product or service bought from Habitat's partner firms (US$, present value)
rows.explainer: Product and service buyers pay market prices; their surplus is the better quality, fit or advice they get over what they would have bought anyway (a few percent to a tenth of a $200 to $800 purchase of cement, roofing, water tanks or a builder's services). Best $20, range $5 to $80: well below a borrower's, so the two are no longer valued alike.

rows.label: Value to a market-branch household of what it bought (US$, present value, borrowers and buyers)
rows.explainer: The borrowers' and buyers' surplus weighted by their shares.

rows.label: ln(consumption) gain per person, market branch
rows.formula: (mkt_lac * ln(1 + mkt_value_per_household / hh_lac / (mkt_vs_dir_consumption * cons_fam_lac)) + mkt_eme * ln(1 + mkt_value_per_household / hh_eme / (mkt_vs_dir_consumption * cons_fam_eme)) + mkt_afr * ln(1 + mkt_value_per_household / hh_afr / (mkt_vs_dir_consumption * cons_fam_afr)) + mkt_ap * ln(1 + mkt_value_per_household / hh_ap / (mkt_vs_dir_consumption * cons_fam_ap))) / (mkt_lac + mkt_eme + mkt_afr + mkt_ap)
rows.explainer: Counted once, in the year bought (the surplus is already a present value), per person at each region's own household size and consumption, weighted by the market people in each region, as the direct branch does.

rows.label: Total ln(consumption) gain per person (both branches, people-weighted)
rows.explainer: For reading; each branch's own gain is used below.

rows.label: Spillover benefits to non-recipients, as a share of recipients' benefits
rows.explainer: Local builders, masons and material sellers earn from the work, as neighbours gain from cash transfers' spending (GiveWell's adjusted Egger et al. 2022 spillover is about 0.7 for cash in Kenya). Housing money buys more imported or factory goods (cement, roofing sheets) than cash does, and the evidence for construction is weaker, so 0.1, range 0 to 0.4. Applied to the direct branch only: market purchases are trades, not new spending.

rows.label: Deaths averted as a share of consumption benefits
rows.explainer: Deaths only: cement floors, latrines and improved stoves cut children's diarrhoea and respiratory illness (Piso Firme, Cattaneo et al. 2009, measured illness, not deaths), so some child deaths are averted where that is the work. GiveWell's mortality effect for cash is about 0.2 of consumption value; Habitat's floors, latrines and stoves are a small part of its direct work, so 0.03, range 0 to 0.1; × your value of a life. Illness itself is in unmodelled_benefits_adj. Direct branch only.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.explainer: The outcome-weighted average of the two branch adjustments, for reading only; each branch applies its own.

rows.label: Direct branch: what a housing dollar is worth to the family against a cash dollar
rows.explainer: One question: how much a dollar of housing help is worth against a dollar of cash. Families choose incremental improvements they want and would otherwise save for (a room, a floor), so the help is close to inframarginal, where in-kind transfers are valued near their cost (Cunha 2014, American Economic Journal: Applied, on Mexico's food transfers); a fixed design and timing lowers it a little. 0.85, range 0.6 to 1.

rows.label: Market branch: reliability of Habitat's count of partners' customers
rows.explainer: One question: how reliable Habitat's count of partners' customers is (partners' own reports, aggregated by Habitat with no stated method; some customers counted by more than one partner or programme). 0.8, range 0.5 to 1. The surplus is already money-metric, so no in-kind discount.

rows.label: Direct branch: share of the housing improvement that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Poor families improve their homes themselves, slowly, room by room (Habitat's own description of incremental building); some of what Habitat helps with would have been built a few years later, and some disaster shelter would have come from other agencies. 0.75, range 0.5 to 0.9.

rows.label: Market branch: share of the partners' housing sales that exist because of Habitat
rows.explainer: Of the partners' housing sales Habitat counts, the share that wouldn't have happened without its advice and seed capital. Habitat's partners are commercial lenders and firms whose housing business mostly predates or outgrows Habitat; the six randomised trials of new microcredit access (Banerjee, Karlan and Zinman 2015, American Economic Journal: Applied) found that opening a lender raised borrowing only modestly, much of it replacing other credit. Habitat helped open housing lines (MicroBuild's investees later 'mobilized a cumulative US$1.26 billion'), but that is leverage, not a counterfactual. 0.3, range 0.1 to 0.6.

rows.label: Share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.explainer: The outcome-weighted average of the two branch adjustments, for reading only; each branch applies its own.

rows.label: Direct branch: HFHI's share of the resources behind the subsidy counted
rows.explainer: The direct branch counts only the housing HFHI's own transfers pay for, but national organisations deliver it with staff and offices partly funded by local fundraising and institutional donors, and Global Village and local volunteers work on the same homes (families' own labour is netted in the subsidy per family, so it isn't counted here). HFHI's share of those resources: 0.8, range 0.6 to 0.95, the same convention as the US model's share by resources (Convention 2).

rows.label: Market branch: HFHI's share of Habitat's resources behind the market work
rows.explainer: The households Habitat counts in market development come from the whole network's market work: HFHI's Terwilliger Center and MicroBuild, and national organisations' own housing-finance and materials programmes, funded partly by others (the Mastercard Foundation, USAID until 2025, local donors). HFHI is the largest part: 0.7, range 0.4 to 1. The market work is mostly HFHI staff time, not transfers, so it doesn't move with the direct branch's share of the transfers. The partners' own capital is repaid by their customers, so it isn't a subsidy.

rows.label: This charity's share of the resources behind the outcome (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.explainer: The outcome-weighted average of the two branch shares, for reading only; each branch applies its own.

rows.label: Share of credit used (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared. Each branch applies its own.

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: Below 1 because some of HFHI's international grants pass on institutional money that would reach the national organisations anyway, beyond what the shares by resources already handle. Anchored on GiveWell's 0.85 to 0.95 for its top charities; high end 1. Home Equals is modelled in habitat-for-humanity-charityevals-awareness; none of its money enters this model.

rows.label: Direct branch: counted less where the outcome isn't measured for Habitat
rows.explainer: Thin (templates.md Convention 12): the families reached are HFHI's transfers over a judged subsidy per family, and the value is a judgment anchored on research on housing improvements elsewhere (Piso Firme), not a count of Habitat's own families or a controlled evaluation of its work. The shared missing-data discount.

rows.label: Market branch: counted less where the outcome isn't measured for Habitat
rows.explainer: Thin: Habitat's count of partners' customers, with no stated method, and a surplus per household that is a judgment anchored on the microcredit trials, not measured for these customers. The shared missing-data discount.

rows.label: Direct branch: all adjustments combined
Market branch: all adjustments combined
Missing-data step (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.explainer: The outcome-weighted average of the branches' missing-data steps, for reading only; both branches are thin, so this is the shared discount.

rows.label: All adjustments combined (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.explainer: The outcome-weighted average of the two branches' combined adjustments, for reading only; each branch applies its own.

rows.label: Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Not modelled, as a share of the modelled value: (+) illness averted by floors, latrines and stoves (Piso Firme: large falls in children's parasites and diarrhoea, Cattaneo et al. 2009), +5%; (+) security of tenure from Habitat's land and titling help and professional services (49,985 people; civil-society facilitation is with Home Equals in the awareness model), +3%; (+) homes that withstand later storms and floods (Habitat's disaster-resilient designs), +3%; (−) families who default on revolving-fund loans or are moved for relocation sites lose part of the value, −2%. Habitat's Home Equals advocacy is no longer here: it is modelled with HFHI's public awareness and education programme (habitat-for-humanity-charityevals-awareness). The high end allows for larger health effects.
